hints: Calculate the work done against the constant resistance force of $50\text{ N}$ over the distance of $24\text{ m}$: $W_{\text{res}} = 50 \times 24 = 1200\text{ J}$.
The athlete produces $1541\text{ J}$ of work to overcome resistance and increase kinetic energy from $u = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ to $v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
State the work-energy balance: $WD = \Delta KE + W_{\text{res}}$, so $1541 = \frac{1}{2}m(6^2 - 5^2) + 1200$, and solve for the mass $m$.
walkthrough:
Calculate the work done against the resistance force:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = 50 \times 24 = 1200\text{ J}$$
teacher_walkthrough: Apply the work-energy principle to the athlete's motion along the horizontal track:

The mechanical energy supplied by the athlete is spent partly in overcoming resistance and partly in increasing kinetic energy:
$$WD_{\text{athlete}} = \Delta KE + W_{\text{resistance}}$$

Step 1: Compute the work done against resistance over the distance of $s = 24\text{ m}$:
$$W_{\text{resistance}} = R \times s = 50 \times 24 = 1200\text{ J}$$

Step 2: Express the change in kinetic energy in terms of mass $m$:
$$\Delta KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^2 - \frac{1}{2}mu^2 = \frac{1}{2}m(v^2 - u^2)$$
Given initial speed $u = 5\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and final speed $v = 6\text{ m s}^{-1}$:
$$v^2 - u^2 = 6^2 - 5^2 = 36 - 25 = 11$$
$$\Delta KE = \frac{1}{2}m(11) = 5.5m\text{ J}$$

Step 3: Substitute the work and energy terms into the work-energy equation:
$$1541 = 5.5m + 1200$$
Therefore, the mass of the athlete is $62\text{ kg}$.
